body:
# Independent audit of critical covers and global support stress

Audited files:

* `candidate b989614dc4f86228`
* `candidate 21a9da879344205f`
* the finite cone description in
  `candidate 94a1565e143d393e`

The intended conditional results pass this audit. The actual-family
hypothesis should be stated explicitly before Sections 5–7 of the critical
cover note, with a lattice-convex fixed projection when claiming an induced
mixed-integer set or the lattice convexity of its positive-volume support.
The support stress requires a maximizing family of **full-dimensional
polytopal** fibers. This audit does not remove that assumption, prove a
polytopal extremizer exists, or extend fixed-projection attainment to hollow
projections. The measures here are mixed \(d\)-volume with positive total
mass, not an intrinsic \(q<d\) replacement.

## 1. Cap compactification is valid

Normalize each nonvertical cap's continuous component to a unit vector.
Finite fiber index sets permit simultaneous extended-real limits of all
affine threshold evaluations. Let \(I\) be the indices with finite limits.
The image of the evaluation map \(E_I\) is a closed finite-dimensional
linear subspace. Choosing \(w_0\) with the limiting finite evaluations
and a right inverse \(J\) on that image gives
\[
 v_l=w_l-w_0-J(E_I(w_l-w_0)),\qquad E_Iv_l=0.
\]
The correction tends to zero. Therefore evaluations at the other indices
still diverge with the prescribed signs. One late \(v_l\) has all those
strict signs; a sufficiently large finite multiple added to \(w_0\)
saturates every infinite threshold outside any fixed common fiber ball,
while preserving all finite evaluations exactly.

This is a genuine ambient halfspace realization of the limiting cap
restrictions. It is not an invalid assumption that unbounded integer
normal coefficients themselves converge. At finite thresholds the
limiting continuous normal remains unit, so the boundary has zero
\(d\)-volume in every fiber; dominated convergence gives exact cap mass
convergence. Zero-volume fibers do not affect that statement. Their
points are still retained by the closed-graph membership argument.

The finite-cover limiting argument is also valid for an uncountable
\(S\): the cap sequences are fixed first, and then for each point an
infinite subsequence of memberships in one of the finitely many caps
proves its membership in that cap's limit. No common subsequence depending
simultaneously on all points is required.

## 2. Capacities are attained and continuous, including vertical limits

For
\[
 c_z(u,t)=\inf_a\mu\{(w,x):a\cdot(w-z)+u\cdot x\ge t\},\quad |u|=1,
\]
the compactification retains the finite threshold at index \(z\), exactly
equal to \(t\). Thus the limiting realization remains admissible in the
same infimum, proving attainment. For varying \((u_l,t_l)\), upper
semicontinuity follows by keeping one attaining integer normal fixed.
For lower semicontinuity, use attaining normals along a subsequence
realizing the lower limit, then compactify; its limiting mass is at least
the limiting capacity. These two statements prove continuity.

A vertical cap through the candidate index can be strongly tilted with
any unit continuous normal. With a sufficiently large finite coefficient,
the strictly included and excluded indices retain their classifications;
the boundary indices are merely cut. Its mass is no greater than that of
the vertical cap. This verifies
\[
 D_z(x)=\min_{|u|=1}c_z(u,u\cdot x)
\]
without losing potentially minimizing limits with diverging integer
normals. The minimum exists by continuity on the sphere.

## 3. Interior centers and uniform active-normal ascent

For an actual convex family, the minimal-face argument in the critical
cover note is sound. A positive-volume fiber somewhere on the minimal
projection face forces a positive-volume fiber at its relative-interior
index, by strictly positive barycentric weights. A boundary point of that
fiber is a relative boundary point of the face body. A nonzero relative
supporting functional there must have a nonzero continuous component;
a purely integer functional could not support nontrivially at an interior
projection point. Its outward cap has zero \(d\)-volume on every face
fiber. A large multiple of an exposing projection functional excludes the
finitely many off-face fibers. Thus the claimed zero-depth statement is
valid, including the zero-volume fiber case.

Conversely, a small ball about an interior fiber point gives positive
depth directly. Each fiber maximizer is consequently interior when the
fiber has positive volume.

Suppose a vector \(v\) has strictly negative scalar products with all
active unit continuous normals at such a maximizer. The strict inequality
persists uniformly on a neighborhood of the compact active set. Moving
the center by \(tv\) decreases each corresponding threshold by at least
\(\eta t\), uniformly. A fixed ball in the candidate fiber supplies a
slab volume at least \(c_0t>0\), independent of the integer normal. Other
fibers cannot lose mass when the same threshold decreases. Thus every
integer-normal choice gains at least \(c_0t\), and so does its infimum.
On the compact complement of that neighborhood the original directional
capacities have a uniform positive gap above the minimum. Uniform
continuity preserves this gap for small \(t\). The ascent contradiction
therefore proves balanced active normals with no hidden uniformity gap.

Carathéodory's selection of at most \(d+1\) active continuous normals then
gives caps whose weighted continuous margins sum to zero on the entire
candidate fiber plane. At least one margin is nonnegative at every point,
so those closed caps cover the whole plane. The two-cap construction on
zero-volume fibers also works, using their minimal projection face.
Hence the resulting finite cap family covers \(P\times\mathbb R^d\),
not merely the original bounded body.

That stronger cover makes the fixed-budget maximum-volume consequence
valid without additional support constraints: a competitor of larger
total volume would have strictly smaller normalized depth, contradicting
the stipulated attained depth minimum.

## 4. Finite fan and common erosion

For a polytope, the inner parallel body is obtained by decreasing all
original unit-normal facet offsets by \(t\). Each candidate vertex is
affine in \(t\), and its feasibility is governed by finitely many affine
conditions. For sufficiently small positive \(t\), all combinatorial
incidences are constant; fixed facet normals then make the normal fan
constant. A common refinement of these fans and the original fans over
all fibers, followed by a simplicial refinement, gives the required
finite support coordinate space. The erosion support values are affine
in \(t\) on its rays, including at \(t=0\) by continuity.

The support-convexity and compatibility inequalities are indeed finite,
linear, and homogeneous on this space. Checking the latter on fan rays
is sufficient because each function is linear on every fan cone. Active
rows \(A_0\) therefore give the exact feasible one-sided cone
\(D=\{\delta:A_0\delta\ge0\}\); inactive rows stay satisfied for small
positive perturbations. Full-dimensionality persists by Hausdorff
continuity and a positive inradius in each of the finitely many fibers.

Common erosion preserves compatibility by the exact identity
\[
 \sum_w p_w(K_w\mathbin{\ominus}tB)+tB
   =\sum_w p_w[(K_w\mathbin{\ominus}tB)+tB]
   \subset\sum_w p_wK_w\subset K_z.
\]
Thus its derivative \(e\) belongs to \(D\). At every original unit-normal
facet, \(e_z(n_F)=-1\). No equality between an erosion support function
and \(h_K-t\) in all directions is assumed or needed.

## 5. Coincident facets and strict budget descent

The swept-prism derivatives have the correct signs. If the original
polytope lies inside a cap with a coincident facet, an outward facet
motion adds no retained cap mass, whereas an inward motion loses it:
the contribution is \(|F|\min(\delta(n_F),0)\). If it lies outside the
cap, the contribution is \(|F|\max(\delta(n_F),0)\).

Away from coincidences, the coefficient is
\(|F\cap\operatorname{int}H|\). Edges, transverse facet/cap intersections,
and newly appearing zero-area facets contribute only \(o(t)\). A fixed
fan makes vertex motions affine, so these are the usual finite
polytope swept-prism estimates, including nonsimple original vertices.

The finite set \(G_j\) independently permits coefficient zero or
\(|F|\) at each coincidence. It may contain choices not simultaneously
realized by any one perturbation direction. This causes no error: it is
used as an upper bound on every actual directional derivative. Its
convex hull permits the full interval \([0,|F|]\) of trace coefficients.

For every positive-mass cap there is a facet portion of positive
\((d-1)\)-area strictly inside the cap. To see this, the cap threshold
is strictly below the maximum of its unit normal on some full-dimensional
fiber. A facet incident to a maximizing point has a relatively open
portion still strictly above that threshold. In dimension one this is
the corresponding endpoint with counting area one. This noncoincident
facet portion contributes a strictly negative amount under erosion.
All other selected facet contributions under erosion are nonpositive.
Thus **every** member of **every** active \(G_j\) is strictly negative on
the same direction \(e\). The needed strict-decrease qualification is
proved, not assumed.

## 6. Farkas certificate and multiplier normalization

If \(\delta\in D\), all \(L(\delta)\le0\) for \(L\in\bigcup_jG_j\),
and \(L_0(\delta)>0\), then \(\delta+\varepsilon e\) remains in \(D\).
For small positive \(\varepsilon\), its objective derivative is still
positive and all finitely many active cap derivative bounds are strictly
negative. A sufficiently small support perturbation respects the active
budgets, keeps all slack budgets by continuity, and increases volume.
This contradicts the assumed actual maximum.

The polar cone of
\(\{\delta:A_0\delta\ge0,\ L(\delta)\le0\ \forall L\in\bigcup G_j\}\)
therefore contains \(L_0\). The finite Farkas alternative gives, with the
correct sign,
\[
 L_0=\sum_j\lambda_j L_j-\eta^TA_0,
 \qquad\lambda_j\ge0,\quad\eta\ge0,\quad L_j\in\operatorname{conv}G_j.
\]
This equation is an identity on the chosen support coordinate subspace;
any coordinate equalities are understood as defining that subspace.
The objective coefficient is one. Evaluating at the dilation direction
\(h_*\), for which \(A_0h_*=0\) and \(L_0(h_*)=dM>0\), proves that
some cap multiplier is positive.

This is a valid necessary stress certificate. It should not be described
as selecting one ordinary differentiable cap gradient at every
coincidence: the convexified trace choices are essential.

## 7. Translation and Euler identities, with both boundary traces

For a cap \(u\cdot x\ge t\), \(|u|=1\), let \(s\) be its effective
section area in the stress note. At a transverse interior section,
the divergence theorem on the truncated polytope gives
\[
 L(c\text{ as a translation})=s\,u\cdot c,
 \qquad L(h_K)=d|K\cap H|+t s. \tag{2}
\]
The same formulas at a coincidence can be verified explicitly:

* If \(K\subset H\), the coincident facet has outward normal \(-u\),
  support value \(-t\), and effective section
  \(s=(1-\theta)|F|\). The other facet normal vectors sum to
  \(|F|u\). Adding the retained coefficient \(\theta|F|\) on this facet
  gives the translation equation in (2). Removing fraction
  \(1-\theta\) of its Euler contribution \(-t|F|\) gives
  \(d|K|+t(1-\theta)|F|\), as claimed.
* If \(K\) lies outside \(H\), the coincident facet has outward normal
  \(u\), support value \(t\), and effective section \(s=\theta|F|\).
  The cap has zero \(d\)-volume, and both equations in (2) follow from
  the single retained facet term.

These calculations also cover negative \(t\); no favorable sign of the
offset has been inserted. Strictly separated caps and lower-dimensional
contacts have effective section zero and satisfy the same identities.

Ordinary affine fiber translations are lineality directions of the
support cone, so the stated global translation and shear balances
follow. Evaluating at dilation eliminates the homogeneous compatibility
stress and gives exactly
\[
 dM=d\sum_j\lambda_j\mu(H_j)
              +\sum_{j,z}\lambda_j t_j(z)s_{j,z}.
\]
For active masses \(\beta M\), its normalized form in the stress note is
therefore correct. It remains an identity; no bound on its signed offset
term follows from this audit.

## 8. Additional balance equations from the full recession space

The balance statement admits a useful rigorous strengthening. The exact
lineality of the compatible support cone consists of the arrays
\[
 \ell_z(u)=u\cdot h(z),\qquad
 h\in\mathcal L(P)\otimes\mathbb R^d.
\]
One direction follows because these are translations preserving every
convex representation landing in \(P\). Conversely, if a support array
and its negative both belong to the cone, each fiber has zero width
in every direction and is a singleton. Compatibility of both signs
then says exactly that its point map belongs coordinatewise to
\(\mathcal L(P)\). All these arrays are linear on the fixed fan.

Define the vector force at an index by
\[
 f_z=\sum_j\lambda_j s_{j,z}u_j.
\]
Evaluating the stress on these lineality directions and using the first
identity in (2) yields
\[
 \sum_z g(z)f_z=0\qquad\hbox{for every }g\in\mathcal L(P). \tag{3}
\]
Equivalently, each coordinate of the force array lies in
\(\mathcal L(P)^\perp\). Constant and ordinary affine coordinate tests
recover the balances already present in the stress note. For a hollow
projection, nonaffine members of \(\mathcal L(P)\) can impose additional
equations. For a projection consisting only of extreme points, they give
\(f_z=0\) separately at every index.

This strengthening remains subject to the same actual-maximizer,
polytopality, and positive fiber-volume hypotheses. It provides no
automatic control of the Euler offset or of the number of active caps.
